en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Jaya.
Vyāsa, the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart...
The world drinks the merit of the honey of speech that has fallen from his lotus-like mouth.
Janamejaya said:
"Having thus heard of the battle with clubs (*mausala-yuddha*) within the clans of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas..."
"What did the Pāṇḍavas do when Kṛṣṇa had thus departed for heaven?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Upon hearing of the great slaughter of the Vṛṣṇis, the Kuru king..."
Having resolved to depart, he spoke these words to Arjuna:
"O high-minded one, Time ripens all beings indeed;
I consider the renunciation of action [to be the way], and you too ought to see it thus."
Thus addressed, the heroic son of Kuntī, saying "Time! Time!", followed those words of his eldest brother.
And Bhīmasena, as well as the twins, having understood Arjuna’s intention, [did the same].
They followed that word which was spoken by Savyasācin. Then, having summoned Yuyutsu and desiring to depart for the sake of dharma,
Yudhiṣṭhira handed over the entire kingdom to the son of the Vaiśya woman.
Having consecrated that King Parikṣit in his own kingdom,
the king, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, afflicted by grief, spoke to Subhadrā:
"This son of your son shall be the king of the Kurus."
Vajra shall be the king of the remnants of the Yadus; Parikṣit shall rule in Hastināpura, while the Yādava Vajra shall rule in Śakraprastha.
You must protect King Vajra, and do not set your mind upon unrighteousness.
Having spoken thus to the wise Vāsudeva,
to his aged maternal uncle, and likewise to Rāma and the others,
the righteous Dharmarāja, together with his mothers, performed the water-libation rites without weariness.

Then, with great effort, he performed *śrāddha* rites for all of them according to the prescribed rules, dedicating them to Dvaipāyana, Nārada, Mārkaṇḍeya rich in asceticism, Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, and Hari.
Having praised the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, he served delicious food;
he gave jewels, garments, villages, horses, and even chariots,
as well as women and hundreds of thousands of cows, to the foremost of the twice-born.
Having honored his teacher Kṛpa with wealth and respect,
and having summoned him, O best of the Bharatas, that most excellent of the Bharatas then seated him upon a throne and gave him his disciple Parikṣit.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira,
the royal seer, having summoned all his subjects, explained everything he intended to do. Upon hearing his words, the people of the city and the countryside [were moved].
With deeply agitated minds, they did not welcome those words;
"This must not be done," they said to that lord of men,
yet the king did not act accordingly, for he understood the law of the passage of time.
Then, having obtained the consent of the people of the city and the countryside,
the righteous-souled one resolved to depart; and at that time, his brothers were engaged in a dispute concerning the sale of a property.
The desire for wealth arose simultaneously for the lords of the earth from their territories;
and perceiving that the Kali Yuga had arrived, Sahadeva, as if laughing,
said to the king, "O Bhārata, Dharma has indeed perished."
"And the king, O monarch, became dejected, thinking: 'Enough of my life. When Govinda, the upholder of dharma, had thus departed, O King, then that Kuru king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma—"
Having cast off the ornaments from their bodies,
they took up garments of bark; Bhīma, Arjuna, the twins, and the illustrious Draupadī likewise all took up the bark garments, O lord of men.
O bull of the Bharatas, having duly performed the final sacrifice,
those bulls among men cast their sacred fires into the waters and set forth.
Then all the women wept aloud upon seeing those foremost of men.
They set out with Draupadī as the sixth, just as they had previously departed when defeated at dice;
and all the brothers felt great joy regarding their departure,
having ascertained Yudhiṣṭhira’s intention and observed the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis.
The five brothers, Kṛṣṇā as the sixth, and a dog as the seventh—
King Yudhiṣṭhira, with himself as the seventh, departed from Hastināpura,
followed for a great distance by all the citizens as well as the women of the inner apartments.
And no one was able to say to him, "Turn back!
Then all the men dwelling in the city turned back,
as did Kṛpa and the others, who surrounded Yuyutsu.
Ulūpī, the daughter of the serpent race, entered the Gaṅgā, O Kauravya; Citrāṅgadā departed toward the city of Maṇipūra;
and the remaining mothers surrounded Parikṣit.
Then the high-souled Pāṇḍavas and the illustrious Draupadī,
having observed their fast, O Kauravya, set out facing the east;
those great-souled ones, disciplined in yoga, had attained the dharma of renunciation.
They traversed many lands, as well as rivers and mountains.
Yudhiṣṭhira went at the head, Bhīma followed immediately after him, Arjuna followed right behind him, and the twins followed in their proper order.

Behind them, O best of the Bharatas, went Draupadī, the most excellent of women, dark-complexioned with eyes like lotus petals and possessed of beautiful hips. And a single dog followed the Pāṇḍavas as they set out for the forest.

In due course, those heroes reached the Lauhitya, that ocean of waters. O great king, Dhananjaya did not release his divine bow, the Gāṇḍīva, nor those two inexhaustible quivers, out of greed for the jewels.
There they beheld Agni standing before them like a mountain, blocking their path, manifest in a human form. Then that seven-flamed god spoke these words to the Pāṇḍavas:
"O heroes, sons of Pāṇḍu, know me to be the Fire-god!
O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, O Bhīmasena, scorcher of foes,
O Arjuna, and you two heroic sons of the Aśvins, listen to my words!"
"I am Agni, O best of the Kurus; by me was the Khandava forest consumed through the power of Arjuna as well as that of Narayana.
This brother of yours, Phalguna, possesses the Gandiva, the supreme weapon."

Let him abandon [the kingdom] and go to the forest; there is no purpose whatsoever to be gained by this [wheel]. As for that jewel-wheel which was situated with the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, it has departed, but in due course it will surely come back into his hand.
"This Gāṇḍīva, the best of bows, was previously obtained by me from Varuṇa for the sake of Pārtha; let it now be given back to Varuṇa himself.
Then all those brothers urged Dhanañjaya.
He cast that [bow] into the water, as well as those two inexhaustible great quivers. O Bhārata, just as a sound is produced by a cloud in the sky,
so indeed was the sound of the Gāṇḍīva as it was being thrown into the water.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the fire vanished right there;
and those heroic Pāṇḍavas proceeded from there facing the south. Then they [went] along the northern shore of the salt-water ocean.
O tiger among the Bharatas, they went toward the south-western direction;
O tiger among the Bharatas, they traveled along the shore of the salt waters.
Then, turning back again, they proceeded toward the south-west.
Then they returned once more toward the western direction and beheld Dvārakā submerged by the ocean,
its great land made into a sacred ford (tīrtha) by the placement of the marks of Hari’s feet.
Worshipping Janārdana with their minds, those blameless ones,
the best of the Bharatas, who were devoted to the practice of yoga, turned back toward the north and proceeded,
desiring to perform a circumambulation of the earth.
17,002.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having restrained their minds, they set out toward the northern direction.
Having bathed at the Brāhmaṇī [tirtha], they beheld the God stationed within the water.
Having gone to Madhyamāṃśa Śiva and beheld the mighty Rudra,
and having bathed at the five Prayāgas and gone to the auspicious Himagiri,
one should pay homage to Īśāna and bathe in the auspicious Haṃsodaka.
Having beheld the god of gods at Kedāra and having touched him with great effort,
and having offered the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) according to the injunctions and indeed satisfied the ancestors and the gods,
he drank the water according to the rite and then proceeded to Nandā.
Having blocked the great path, they went to the Himavat;
and those engaged in yoga beheld the great mountain Himavat.
As they were crossing it, they also saw a sea of sand.
They beheld the great mountain Meru, the best of peaked mountains. As all of them, practitioners of yoga, were traveling swiftly,
Yājñasenī, having fallen from her yoga, dropped down onto the surface of the earth.
Seeing her fallen, the mighty Bhīmasena looked toward Yājñasenī and spoke to Dharmarāja:
"O scorcher of foes, no unrighteousness whatsoever has been committed by this princess."
"What indeed was the cause, O King, that Kṛṣṇā fell to the ground?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"She had a great partiality, especially for Dhanañjaya."
"O best of men, she is now enjoying the fruit of that [act] from the very beginning.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having spoken thus, the king, the son of Dharma, departed without looking back at her."
Having composed his mind, the wise and righteous Sahadeva, that bull among men, then descended to the surface of the earth. Seeing him fallen, Bhīma spoke to the king.
"He who was among all of us devoted in service and free from egoism—
this son of Mādravatī, why has he fallen to the earth?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The righteous Sahadeva, the best among all the wise,
did not consider anyone to be his equal in intelligence. Furthermore, though he knew the three periods of time, he did not reveal my secret.
"Having made a solemn vow, I would never have caused the destruction of people;
because of that transgression, this son of a king has fallen.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus and left Sahadeva behind,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, then departed with his brothers and the dog.
Seeing Draupadī fallen and the Pāṇḍava Sahadeva as well, [he continued on].
Afflicted, brave, and fond of his kinsmen, Nakula fell down.
When that hero of beautiful appearance, Nakula, had fallen,
Bhima then spoke these words once more to the king.
"This Nakula, whose nature is unimpaired, who obeys our commands, and who is peerless in beauty in the world— this very brother has fallen upon the earth.
When Bhīmasena had spoken thus, Yudhiṣṭhira replied.
The righteous-souled one, the best among all the wise, said regarding Nakula:
"In beauty, there is no one equal to me"—this was his view;
and "I alone am superior"—this remained fixed in his mind.
"Nakula has fallen from that [chariot]; come, O Vṛkodara!
Whatever is ordained for each, O hero, that he must inevitably experience.
Then, seeing them fallen, the Pāṇḍava whose horses are white (Arjuna) [acted].
Then, tormented by grief, that slayer of enemy heroes fell down after him. When that tiger among men, possessed of the splendor of Śakra, had fallen—
unassailable and dying— Bhīma spoke to the king.
"I do not recall this high-souled one ever speaking an untruth, even in jest. Now, whose influence is it that has caused him to fall to the ground?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I shall surely consume my enemies in a single day," so Arjuna spoke;
yet he did not accomplish that, for which he fell from his status as one who prides himself on heroism. This Phalguna held all wielders of the bow in contempt.
"And as it has been said, so it must be done by one who desires prosperity.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, King Bhīma set forth and then fell down.
Having fallen, Bhīma said to the Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O King, look! I, your beloved, have fallen.
Tell me, if you know, for what reason has this fall occurred?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"You have eaten excessively, O Pārtha, and you boast of your vital strength; because you disregard the Supreme, you have fallen to the earth."
17,002.026 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to him, the mighty-armed one departed without looking back;
only that single dog followed him, which I have described to you many times.
17,003.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śakra, making heaven and earth resound on all sides,
approached Pārtha in his chariot and said to him, "Ascend!"
Seeing his brothers fallen, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, tormented by grief, spoke these words to the Thousand-eyed One:
"My brothers have fallen here; let them come with me."
"O Lord of the Gods, I do not wish to go to heaven without my brothers.
O Purandara, this princess is delicate and deserves happiness;
let her go with us—may you grant your permission for that."
Indra said:
"O bull of the Bharata lineage, do not grieve; you shall see all your brothers and sons together with Kṛṣṇā, having gone ahead to the third heaven."
"O bull of the Bharatas, having cast off their human bodies, they have gone [to heaven].
You, however, shall go to heaven with this very body; of this there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of the past and the future, this dog has been constantly devoted to me;
let him go with me, for my mind is set on compassion.
Indra said:
"O King, you have today attained immortality, equality with me, complete prosperity, great fame, and the pleasures of heaven."
"Abandon the dog; there is no cruelty in this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Thousand-eyed One, it is ignoble for a noble man [to do so]."
"Noble one, this difficult task can indeed be accomplished.
May I not have union with that splendor for whose sake I would abandon my devoted people."
Indra said:
"In the heavenly world, there is no place for those who behave like dogs;
the Krodhavaśas carry away the merit of their sacrifices and charitable works."
"Therefore, O Dharmarāja, having deliberated, let it be done;
abandon the dog, for there is no cruelty in this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
They say that the abandonment of a devotee is an extreme sin,
equal in this world to the act of killing a Brahmin;
therefore, I shall never, under any circumstances today—
Seeking my own happiness, O Mahendra, I shall abandon this one who is terrified, devoted, and cries out "there is no other!", who has come to me,
exhausted, seeking protection, and desiring life.
"Even at the cost of my life, I shall never strive to release you;
this is indeed my eternal vow.
Indra said:
"Those under the power of anger carry away what has been seen by a dog— whether it be a gift, a sacrifice, an offering, or an oblation.
Therefore, make this renunciation of the dog."
"By abandoning Śunaḥśepha, you shall attain the world of the gods;
O hero, having abandoned your brothers and even your beloved Kṛṣṇā, you have attained this world through your own deed."
17,003.013c "And yet you do not abandon this dog; how is it that, though established in total renunciation, you are now bewildered?
17,003.014 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"There is neither alliance nor enmity with mortals who are dead; this is the established conclusion in the worlds.
Therefore, it is not possible for me to bring them back to life."
Therefore, the abandonment of those [three] was not for the sake of those who were still living:
the returning of one who has sought refuge,
the killing of a woman, and the theft of a Brahmin’s property.
"O Śakra, treachery toward friends— those four,
as well as the abandonment of those who have been devoted, are considered by me to be equal.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of the King of Dharma,
the Blessed One, whose very nature is dharma, spoke with affection to Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of men:
With gentle words joined with praise: "O Indra among kings, you are well-born in the conduct and wisdom of your father,
O Bhārata, as evidenced by this compassion toward all beings."
"O son, long ago in the Dvaitavana forest you were tested by me when your brothers were slain while striving for water;
there you abandoned both your brothers, Bhīma and Arjuna."
Desiring equality with your two mothers, you indeed wish for Nakula to remain alive;
yet, thinking "this dog is devoted," you abandoned the chariot of the gods.
Therefore, O lord of men, there is no one equal to you in heaven.
"Therefore, O Bhārata, imperishable worlds await you in your own body;
O best of the Bharatas, you have attained the divine and unsurpassed goal.
Then Dharma, Śakra, the Maruts, and the two Aśvins [will appear]."
Having placed the Pāṇḍava upon the chariot, the gods and the celestial ṛṣis departed on their own celestial vehicles; those perfected beings (siddhas) travel at will,
all of them stainless, pure, and possessed of merit in speech, thought, and action.
Having mounted that chariot, the king, the enhancer of the Kuru lineage,
ascended swiftly, enveloping heaven and earth with his splendor.
Then Nārada, who dwells among the hosts of gods and knows all the worlds, [spoke].
Then Bṛhadvādī, of great speech and great asceticism, spoke these words aloud:
"Even all those royal sages who have assembled here—
the King of the Kurus indeed stands over them, eclipsing their fame."
Enveloping the worlds with his glory, his splendor, and his perfection of conduct,
we have heard of no one other than the Pāṇḍava who has attained [this state] in his own body.
O Lord, those splendors which were seen by you while standing upon the earth—
"Behold these thousands of dwellings belonging to the *karmadevas*.
Having heard Nārada’s words, the righteous king addressed the gods and his own kinsmen, the earthly monarchs, with these words:
"Whether it be auspicious or whether it be evil, that very place which is now my brothers'—that alone I wish to attain; I do not desire any other worlds.
Having heard these words of the king, Purandara, the king of the gods, [replied].
Endowed with compassion, he replied to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Dwell in this place, O Indra among kings, which has been won by your auspicious deeds.
Why do you still cling to human affection?"
"O joy of the Kurus, you have attained the supreme perfection that no other man has ever reached anywhere;
yet even now, O lord of men, your human nature still clings to you."
"Behold this heaven, O Lord, with its gods, ṛṣis, and Siddhas who dwell in the third realm.
But Yudhiṣṭhira,
the wise one, spoke these meaningful words once again to the Lord, the ruler of the gods, who had spoken thus.
"O destroyer of Daityas, I cannot bear to dwell here without them;
I wish to go to that place where my brothers have gone,
where she dwells— tall and dark-complexioned, endowed with the qualities of intelligence and goodness."
Draupadī, the best among women, who is indeed dear to me.
